extracted.intended_audience: psychology researchers, journal editors, and scholars studying peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical investigation of how psychological journals' peer-review processes handle resubmitted (previously published) manuscripts, testing reliability, bias, detection, and editorial decisions in natural journal settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The consistency and dependability of modern peer-review practices; explicitly named in the abstract as a growing concern to be studied directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study measured consistency indirectly by resubmitting published articles and observing reviewer/editor responses; references to measures of interrater agreement (e.g., intraclass correlation coefficient, weighted kappa) are cited in the literature list as relevant statistical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which reviewers and editors can be held responsible for the quality and fairness of their evaluations; listed in the abstract as a key variable of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability is raised as part of broader concerns about modern peer review; the experiment (using resubmissions) probes whether reviewers/editors recognize and correct prior errors or biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Biases affecting reviewers' judgments (e.g., based on author identity, institution, prestige); explicitly listed in the abstract as a central variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resubmission design (fictitious names/institutions) tests for favoritism/penalization related to author/institutional prestige; the choice of articles from prestigious departments and journals with nonblind reviewing probes this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' ability and expertise to detect problems in manuscripts and make appropriate publication recommendations; named in the abstract as a variable of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in practice by whether referees detected that resubmissions were previously published and by the nature of their critiques (e.g., identifying methodological flaws). The study reports low detection (3 of 38) and frequent recommendation against publication when methodological issues were cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of previously published/resubmitted manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of editors and reviewers to detect that a resubmitted manuscript had already been published (here tested using altered manuscripts with fictitious names/institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: of 38 editors and reviewers contacted, only 3 (8%) detected the resubmissions. This detection rate is an explicit metric for assessing peer-review vigilance and editorial checking procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial concurrence with reviewer recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which journal editors follow or concur with referees' recommendations (accept/reject); observed and reported in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical guidance: of evaluated resubmissions, 16 of 18 referees (89%) recommended against publication and the editors concurred; use concurrence rate as a metric of editorial decision-making relative to referee advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for rejection — methodological flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive reasons given for rejecting manuscripts, frequently described in the study as 'serious methodological flaws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many rejections the stated grounds were methodological problems; therefore methodological rigor/validity is a primary evaluative dimension in referee reports and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind versus nonblind refereeing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether refereeing is blind (anonymized) or nonblind (reviewers know author identity) and how that affects review outcomes; the study focused on journals with nonblind refereeing practices and references blind-review debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper situates its sample in journals with nonblind refereeing and cites literature on blind reviewing (e.g., 'Eight APA journals initiate controversial blind reviewing'); compare outcomes across blind/nonblind systems when possible to assess bias and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal selectivity / rejection rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The baseline selectivity of journals (e.g., high rejection rates) as a context for evaluating peer-review decisions; the study sampled journals with ~80% rejection rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use journal rejection rate as contextual information when interpreting referee/editor behavior — high-selectivity journals may exhibit different reviewing standards or gatekeeping behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of author/institutional prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of author identity and institutional affiliation on reviewers' and editors' evaluations; implied by study design selecting articles from 'prestigious and highly productive' departments and by use of fictitious names/institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment tests whether stripping prestige (by substituting fictitious names/institutions) changes outcomes; this criterion examines whether evaluations depend on provenance rather than manuscript content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations of deceptive methods in peer-review research
rubrics_metrics.description: The ethics of using deception (substituting fictitious names/institutions) to study peer review; the study employed this method and references ethics literature (e.g., 'Ethical principles in the conduct of research with human participants').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using deceptive methods to evaluate peer review, researchers should weigh ethical guidelines and potential harms; the paper notes the method and cites relevant ethics discussions in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrater agreement and statistical measures of reviewer agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal statistical evaluation of agreement among reviewers (e.g., intraclass correlation coefficient, weighted kappa) as a way to quantify reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The references cite Bartko (intraclass correlation), Cohen (weighted kappa) and other studies on reviewer agreement; such measures are recommended tools for assessing consistency across referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / openness of refereeing (open or published refereeing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether referee reports are published or refereeing is open, and the potential effects of transparency on review quality and accountability; discussed in references (e.g., 'optional published refereeing', 'open refereeing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider open or published refereeing as an alternative to anonymous review to address accountability and bias; the literature cited includes proposals and experiments with such systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and competence of editors
rubrics_metrics.description: How well qualified editors are to manage peer review and make publication decisions (question posed in referenced literature: 'How qualified are editors?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate editor training, expertise, and decision-making procedures as part of the overall review quality; editorial qualifications can influence concurrence with referees and detection of resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript characteristics influencing acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of manuscripts (e.g., methodological soundness, clarity, novelty, theoretical alignment) that influence reviewers' acceptance decisions; referenced in multiple cited studies on manuscript characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess specific manuscript-level dimensions (methodology, clarity, significance) when judging review outcomes; the study and references indicate empirical effects of manuscript characteristics on reviewer decisions.
